newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Mir crew may fix problems, enter Spektr Thursday.
newsitem.headline: Mir crew may fix problems, enter Spektr Thursday.

text.p: The crew of Russia's troubled Mir space station may enter the airless Spektr module on Thursday but must first fix a computer and re-align the rotating station with the sun, a senior Mission Control official said on Tuesday.

Deputy flight director Viktor Blagov said the cosmonauts would spend the day changing a computer section which crashed on Monday and would also test the system. He said the cosmonauts had been trained to change the section on earth.

"If the tests go fine, they will switch on the computer tomorrow, and will try to bring the ship back into line with the sun immediately," he told Reuters from the Mission Control in Korolyov outside Moscow.
The sortie to Spektr was initially scheduled for Wednesday, but the computer crash made Mission Control delay it.
Blagov said the cosmonauts would have to realign the station to the sun as quickly as possible to avoid running down the batteries, which are needed be run the computer system.
"So we are prepared to abort the attempt (to reboot the computer) and switch off the system again if we see that they are running low on batteries," Blagov said.
In that case the spacewalk could be postponed to Friday or later, he added.
The station has been spinning in orbit since Monday evening, when a computer failure during a docking procedure prompted the station automatically to switch off all but vital life support systems.

It was the third time the station had spun out of control in less than two months and came as a blow to the new Russian crew, who had experienced a relatively trouble-free start to their mission after their predecessors suffered a string of disasters.

Previous computer failures took only a day to fix and officials said on Monday they hoped to put right the most recent failure on Tuesday. Blagov said the current computer repairs could take longer but this was not a cause for concern.

The computer failure meant Mir lost its stable orientation with the sun, which its solar panels need to face to produce energy. Blagov said the station's solar panels were still catching enough energy to supply the life support systems.

"Most of the time solar arrays are getting the sunlight. Only occasionally the cosmonauts have to fire engines to turn the station a bit to increase power supply. We see from the earth when power supply is low and we tell them to go to their spaceship and fire the engines for 10 seconds," Blagov said.
He said firing the engines of the Soyuz spaceship did not mean aligning the station to the sun but only changing its position slightly when solar panels catch no light at all.

Mir has run on partial power since its Spektr module was holed in a collision with a cargo ship on June 25 in the worst accident in its 11-year history. The cosmonauts have to enter the module to re-connect electric cables leading from Spektr's solar panels to the main ship.
